content:
## Analysis

The problem is a **diff-visibility trap** caused by adding new lines to the **end** of `.gitignore`.

Here's what happens in the review tool for PR 830 (`+*.log`):

```
  @@ -1,7 +1,8 @@
   # managed ignore rules     ← line 1 (context)
   *.pyc                     ← line 2 (context)
   .venv/                    ← line 3 (context)
   __pycache__/              ← line 4 (context)
   build/                    ← line 5 (context)
   dist/                     ← line 6 (context)
   logs/                     ← line 7 (context)
   node_modules/             ← line 8 (context)
  +*.log                    ← line 9 (ADDED)
```

The hunk has **8 lines of unchanged context** followed by **1 line of actual change**. By the time a reviewer has scanned those 8 context lines, their eye has already drifted to the next hunk or to scrolling. The new line is literally the last thing in the hunk — and if the hunk sits low on the screen, it's below the fold.

All four incidents in `review_misses.md` followed this same pattern: the new rule was the **last line of the file**, and reviewers' eyes had left the diff before they got to it.

## Recommendation

**Newly added ignore rules should go immediately after the `# managed ignore rules` comment, i.e., at the top of the rule list, not at the bottom.**

```gitignore
# managed ignore rules
<--- NEW RULE GOES HERE --->
*.pyc
.venv/
__pycache__/
build/
dist/
logs/
node_modules/
```

When added at the top, the diff would instead look like:

```
  @@ -1,7 +1,8 @@
   # managed ignore rules     ← line 1 (context)
  +*.log                     ← line 2 (ADDED) — first thing reviewer sees
   *.pyc                     ← line 3 (context)
   .venv/                    ← line 4 (context)
   __pycache__/              ← line 5 (context)
   build/                    ← line 6 (context)
   dist/                     ← line 7 (context)
   logs/                     ← line 8 (context)
   node_modules/             ← line 9 (context)
```

Now the change is the **second line of the hunk** — right after the header comment and right at the top of the hunk where the reviewer's gaze lands first. It's nearly impossible to miss.

### Why this works

- **Eye-tracking pattern**: Reviewers read diffs top-to-bottom; placing the change early in the hunk ensures it's seen before attention wanes.
- **Screen fold**: A change near the hunk's start is visible even when the hunk is long.
- **Convention clarity**: If every team member knows "new rules go after the header," it becomes a shared, checkable habit. A reviewer who sees a rule at the bottom can flag it as a placement violation.

Agreed. Decision: recent additions at the top, directly under the header line, so a reviewer sees what the branch added in the first lines of the diff instead of hunting for a green line at the bottom of a long file. The existing rules keep the order they already have; only new entries go above them.
